metadata.title: Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines
metadata.authors: Nicholas Metropolis, Arianna W. Rosenbluth, Marshall N. Rosenbluth, Augusta H. Teller, Edward Teller
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: PDF first-page title and authors match metadata.json (Metropolis et al. 1953).

nodes.name: Equation of state via canonical-ensemble integration
nodes.statement: Compute the canonical-ensemble equilibrium average $F = \frac{\int F \exp(-E/kT)\, d^{2N}p\, d^{2N}q}{\int \exp(-E/kT)\, d^{2N}p\, d^{2N}q}$ for a system of $N$ interacting particles with two-body potential $V$.
nodes.statement_clean: Evaluate equilibrium averages of observables in the canonical ensemble for an N-particle interacting system, in order to determine the equation of state.

nodes.name: Periodic boundary conditions and minimum distance $d_{AB}$
nodes.statement: The simulation cell is a square containing $N$ particles, replicated periodically. The minimum distance $d_{AB}$ between particles $A$ and $B$ is the shortest distance between $A$ and any periodic image of $B$.
nodes.statement_clean: Defines a periodically replicated square cell and the minimum-image convention for inter-particle distances.

nodes.name: Total potential energy
nodes.statement: $E = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{\substack{j=1\\ j\neq i}}^{N} V(d_{ij})$, where $V$ is the pair potential and $d_{ij}$ the minimum-image distance.
nodes.statement_clean: Pairwise potential energy of the N-particle configuration using the minimum-image distances.

nodes.name: Canonical ensemble average
nodes.statement: $F = \left[\int F\,\exp(-E/kT)\, d^{2N}p\, d^{2N}q\right] / \left[\int \exp(-E/kT)\, d^{2N}p\, d^{2N}q\right]$.
nodes.statement_clean: Equilibrium expectation of property F as a Boltzmann-weighted phase-space integral.

nodes.name: Trial move (proposal)
nodes.statement: Each particle is moved by $X \to X + \alpha \xi_1$, $Y \to Y + \alpha \xi_2$, where $\alpha$ is the maximum displacement and $\xi_1,\xi_2$ are independent random numbers in $(-1,1)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A proposed move displaces a particle uniformly within a square of side $2\alpha$ centred on its current position.

nodes.name: Sample average over moves
nodes.statement: $F = (1/M) \sum_{j=1}^{M} F_j$, where $F_j$ is the value of $F$ after the $j$th attempted move (whether accepted or not).
nodes.statement_clean: Estimator of the ensemble average as the arithmetic mean of the observable along the generated chain.

nodes.name: Radial distribution count $N_m$
nodes.statement: Divide the annulus between $\pi d_0^2$ and $K^2 \pi d_0^2$ into 64 zones of equal area $\Delta A^2$, and let $N_m$ count the pairs of particles whose squared separation $r^2$ lies in zone $m$ ($m=1,\dots,64$).
nodes.statement_clean: Histogram of pair separations used to estimate the radial distribution function.

nodes.name: Cluster integral $A_{i,k}$
nodes.statement: $A_{i,k}$ is the cluster integral over configuration space of $i$ particles connected by $k$ overlap bonds (a bond between $i,j$ if $r_{ij} < d$); primes distinguish topologically different bond patterns of the same $(i,k)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Combinatorial integrals over particle configurations weighted by overlap-bond indicators, used in the virial expansion.

nodes.name: Standing assumptions
nodes.statement: Classical statistics; only two-body forces; spherically symmetric molecular potential; finite $N$ (up to several hundred); periodic boundary conditions.
nodes.statement_clean: Lists the modeling assumptions under which the method and analysis are presented.

nodes.name: Metropolis Monte Carlo algorithm
nodes.statement: Markov-chain Monte Carlo sampler that generates configurations distributed as $\exp(-E/kT)$ by proposing random local moves and accepting them with probability $\min(1, \exp(-\Delta E / kT))$.
nodes.statement_clean: Iterative sampling scheme that draws configurations from the Boltzmann distribution by proposing local moves and accepting with the Metropolis criterion.
output: Sequence of configurations approximately distributed as $\exp(-E/kT)$
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize particles in a configuration. For each cycle, attempt to move each particle in turn: draw $\xi_1,\xi_2 \in (-1,1)$ and propose $X' = X + \alpha\xi_1$, $Y' = Y + \alpha\xi_2$ (with periodic wrap). Compute $\Delta E$. If $\Delta E \leq 0$, accept. Otherwise draw $\xi_3 \in (0,1)$; accept if $\xi_3 < \exp(-\Delta E / kT)$, else reject and keep the old position. In either case, count the (new or old) configuration in the running average $F = (1/M) \sum_j F_j$.

nodes.name: Initialize configuration
nodes.statement: Place the $N$ particles in some configuration (e.g. a regular lattice such as the trigonal lattice of Fig. 2).

nodes.name: Sweep over particles
nodes.statement: Iterate over particles $i = 1, \dots, N$; for each, perform a trial move and acceptance test (steps 3-5), then move on to the next particle.

nodes.name: Propose displacement
nodes.statement: Draw random $\xi_1, \xi_2 \in (-1, 1)$ and set $X \to X + \alpha\xi_1$, $Y \to Y + \alpha\xi_2$. Wrap into the square via the periodicity assumption if necessary.

nodes.name: Metropolis acceptance test
nodes.statement: Compute $\Delta E$. If $\Delta E < 0$, accept the move. Otherwise draw $\xi_3 \in (0,1)$: accept if $\xi_3 < \exp(-\Delta E / kT)$; else reject and restore the old position.

nodes.name: Update running averages
nodes.statement: Whether the move was accepted or not, treat the (new or restored) configuration as a new sample and add $F$ at this configuration to the running average $F = (1/M) \sum_j F_j$.

nodes.name: Repeat until convergence
nodes.statement: Continue cycles until the chain has equilibrated and the desired number of post-equilibration samples has been collected.

nodes.name: Convergence of the Metropolis chain to the canonical distribution
nodes.statement: The Markov chain defined by the trial-move-plus-acceptance rule is ergodic and its stationary distribution is the canonical distribution $\nu_r \propto \exp(-E_r / kT)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Proves that the proposed sampling scheme generates configurations whose long-run distribution is the desired Boltzmann distribution.
assumptions: Symmetric proposal: $P_{rs} = P_{sr}$ (uniform displacement in a square of side $2\alpha$)
A configuration of lower energy is always accepted; a higher-energy move is accepted with probability $\exp(-\Delta E / kT)$
Forbidden (rejected) moves leave the chain at its current state, which is still counted in the average
conclusions: The chain is ergodic: every configuration in the cell can be reached from any other
The ensemble of chain states approaches the canonical distribution $\nu_r \propto \exp(-E_r / kT)$

nodes.name: Proof of convergence to the canonical distribution
nodes.statement:
Combine ergodicity (any configuration is reachable by enough symmetric proposals) with a detailed-balance-style flow argument: between any two states $r,s$, if $
u_r / 
u_s > \exp(-E_r/kT) / \exp(-E_s/kT)$, the net flow $P_{rs}(
u_s \exp(-(E_r-E_s)/kT) - 
u_r)$ moves systems from $r$ to $s$, driving the ensemble to the canonical distribution.

nodes.name: Symmetric proposal $P_{rs} = P_{sr}$
nodes.statement: Because each particle is moved uniformly in a square of side $2\alpha$ centred on its current position, the a priori probability of proposing $r \to s$ equals that of proposing $s \to r$ (both nonzero only when the moved positions lie within each other's proposal squares).

nodes.name: Ergodicity
nodes.statement: Since each particle has positive probability of moving anywhere within its proposal square at each step, a long enough sequence of moves can carry the system from any configuration to any other; configuration space is connected by the chain.

nodes.name: Net flow between two states
nodes.statement:
Assume $E_r > E_s$. The number of systems moving $r 	o s$ in one step is $
u_r P_{rs}$ (all such moves accepted). The number moving $s 	o r$ is $
u_s P_{sr} \exp(-(E_r - E_s)/kT)$. The net flow $r 	o s$ is $P_{rs}(
u_s \exp(-(E_r-E_s)/kT) - 
u_r)$, vanishing iff $
u_r/
u_s = \exp(-(E_r-E_s)/kT)$.

nodes.name: Approach to canonical distribution
nodes.statement: Combining ergodicity with the net-flow expression: deviations from $\nu_r \propto \exp(-E_r / kT)$ generate a restoring flow, so the ensemble must approach the canonical distribution. (Counting rejected moves as a new visit to the original state is essential to avoid distorting the relative weights.)

nodes.name: Choice of maximum displacement $\alpha$
nodes.statement: The argument does not bound the convergence rate. The displacement $\alpha$ must be chosen with care: if too large, most moves are forbidden; if too small, the configuration changes too slowly. Either extreme delays equilibration.

nodes.name: Rigid-sphere simplification
nodes.statement: For rigid spheres, $\Delta E \in \{0, \infty\}$, so the acceptance test reduces to: accept the move unless the moved sphere overlaps another, in which case keep it at the original position.

nodes.name: Virial theorem
nodes.statement: $\left(\sum_i X_i^{(\text{tot})} \cdot r_i\right)_{\text{Av}} = 2PA + \left(\sum_i X_i^{(\text{int})} \cdot r_i\right)_{\text{Av}} = 2 E_{\text{kin}}$, with $E_{\text{kin}} = N m \bar{v}^2 / 2$.
nodes.statement_clean: Clausius virial theorem relating pressure, area, and the average of forces dotted with positions.

nodes.name: Equation of state for two-dimensional rigid spheres
nodes.statement: $PA = E_{\text{kin}}(1 + \pi d_0^2 \bar{n} / 2) = N k T (1 + \pi d_0^2 \bar{n} / 2)$, where $\bar{n}$ is the average density of other particles at the surface of a particle.
nodes.statement_clean: Closed-form expression for the rigid-sphere equation of state in terms of the contact-pair density $\bar{n}$.
assumptions: Two-dimensional system of $N$ rigid spheres of contact distance $d_0$
Velocity-independent two-body potential, so velocities are Maxwellian
conclusions: Determining $\bar{n}$ as a function of area $A$ suffices to determine the equation of state

nodes.name: Two-dimensional rigid-sphere simulation on the MANIAC
nodes.statement: Run with $N = 224$ particles in a unit square, initially in a 14x16 trigonal lattice, with maximum displacement $\alpha = d - d_0$. About 48-64 cycles per value of $\nu \in \{0,1,2,3,4,5,5.5,6,6.25,6.5,7\}$ on the Los Alamos MANIAC (~3 minutes per cycle).
nodes.statement_clean: The actual numerical experiment in the paper: a 224-particle 2D rigid-sphere fluid sampled by the Metropolis algorithm on the MANIAC computer.

nodes.name: Radial distribution function at $\nu = 5$
nodes.statement_clean: Sample radial-distribution-function fit at $\nu=5$ illustrating how $\bar{N}_t$ is extracted and converted into the pressure.

nodes.name: Virial coefficient expansion
nodes.statement_clean: Expansion of the equation of state in powers of inverse area, with cluster-integral coefficients.

nodes.name: Numerical virial expansion
nodes.statement_clean: Numerical four-term virial expansion obtained by combining algebraic and Monte-Carlo evaluations of the $A_{i,k}$.

nodes.name: Agreement of Monte Carlo with virial expansion and free-volume theory
nodes.statement: For two-dimensional rigid spheres, the Monte Carlo equation of state agrees with the free-volume approximation for $A/A_0 < 1.8$ and with the five-term virial expansion for $A/A_0 > 2.5$, with no indication of a phase transition.
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical conclusion: the new Monte Carlo data interpolate between the small-area free-volume regime and the large-area virial regime, with no phase transition seen.
